claim: Nearly 28,000 long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been reported in the human genome.
source: To date, nearly 28,000 long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been reported in the human genome, but less than 1% (~150) has been functionally characterized (Ransohoff et al., 2018; Hon et al., 2017; Quek et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ransohoff et al., 2018; Hon et al., 2017; Quek et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016)

claim: Less than 1% (~150) of lncRNAs have been functionally characterized.
source: To date, nearly 28,000 long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been reported in the human genome, but less than 1% (~150) has been functionally characterized (Ransohoff et al., 2018; Hon et al., 2017; Quek et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ransohoff et al., 2018; Hon et al., 2017; Quek et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016)

claim: Several lncRNAs have been shown to influence cellular physiology in developmental, adult and disease contexts.
source: Several of those have been shown to influence cellular physiology in developmental, adult and disease contexts (Sarropoulos et al., 2019; James, 2015; Prensner et al., 2011; Castellanos-Rubio et al., 2016; Perry and Ulitsky, 2016; Lorenzi et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Sarropoulos et al., 2019; James, 2015; Prensner et al., 2011; Castellanos-Rubio et al., 2016; Perry and Ulitsky, 2016; Lorenzi et al., 2021)

claim: lncRNAs can be classified into genic lncRNAs (overlapping with a protein-coding gene) or intergenic lncRNAs (lincRNAs; no overlap with a protein-coding gene).
source: Depending on their genomic location, lncRNAs can be classified into genic lncRNAs (overlapping with a protein-coding gene) or intergenic lncRNAs (lincRNAs; no overlap with a protein-coding gene) (Ransohoff et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ransohoff et al., 2018)

claim: lncRNAs participate in complex gene-regulatory networks by fine-tuning gene expression in a precise and controlled manner.
source: Together with transcription factors and epigenetic regulators (Hung et al., 2011; Jeon and Lee, 2011; Boque-Sastre et al., 2015), lncRNAs participate in complex gene-regulatory networks by fine-tuning gene expression in a precise and controlled manner (Grote and Herrmann, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hung et al., 2011; Jeon and Lee, 2011; Boque-Sastre et al., 2015; Grote and Herrmann, 2015)

claim: lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression by affecting chromatin structure and folding.
source: In particular, lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression at multiple levels, including chromatin structure and folding (Gupta et al., 2010), activating neighboring (Engreitz et al., 2013) and distal (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014) genes, affecting RNA splicing (Pisignano and Ladomery, 2021), or influencing nuclear compartmentalization (Caudron-Herger and Rippe, 2012; Rinn and Guttman, 2014; Quinodoz and Guttman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gupta et al., 2010)

claim: lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression by activating neighboring genes.
source: In particular, lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression at multiple levels, including chromatin structure and folding (Gupta et al., 2010), activating neighboring (Engreitz et al., 2013) and distal (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014) genes, affecting RNA splicing (Pisignano and Ladomery, 2021), or influencing nuclear compartmentalization (Caudron-Herger and Rippe, 2012; Rinn and Guttman, 2014; Quinodoz and Guttman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Engreitz et al., 2013)

claim: lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression by activating distal genes.
source: In particular, lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression at multiple levels, including chromatin structure and folding (Gupta et al., 2010), activating neighboring (Engreitz et al., 2013) and distal (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014) genes, affecting RNA splicing (Pisignano and Ladomery, 2021), or influencing nuclear compartmentalization (Caudron-Herger and Rippe, 2012; Rinn and Guttman, 2014; Quinodoz and Guttman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014)

claim: lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression by affecting RNA splicing.
source: In particular, lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression at multiple levels, including chromatin structure and folding (Gupta et al., 2010), activating neighboring (Engreitz et al., 2013) and distal (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014) genes, affecting RNA splicing (Pisignano and Ladomery, 2021), or influencing nuclear compartmentalization (Caudron-Herger and Rippe, 2012; Rinn and Guttman, 2014; Quinodoz and Guttman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Pisignano and Ladomery, 2021)

claim: lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression by influencing nuclear compartmentalization.
source: In particular, lncRNAs have been shown to modulate gene expression at multiple levels, including chromatin structure and folding (Gupta et al., 2010), activating neighboring (Engreitz et al., 2013) and distal (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014) genes, affecting RNA splicing (Pisignano and Ladomery, 2021), or influencing nuclear compartmentalization (Caudron-Herger and Rippe, 2012; Rinn and Guttman, 2014; Quinodoz and Guttman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Caudron-Herger and Rippe, 2012; Rinn and Guttman, 2014; Quinodoz and Guttman, 2014)

claim: Long non-coding RNAs have been shown to fine-tune the activation and function of developmental regulators, including transcription factors responsible for maintenance of pluripotency.
source: More specifically, long non-coding RNAs have also been shown to fine-tune the activation and function of developmental regulators, including transcription factors responsible for maintenance of pluripotency (Sheik Mohamed et al., 2010; Ulitsky et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2012), mesoderm specification (Frank et al., 2019) and neuronal differentiation (Xi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Sheik Mohamed et al., 2010; Ulitsky et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2012)

claim: Long non-coding RNAs have been shown to fine-tune the activation and function of developmental regulators involved in mesoderm specification.
source: More specifically, long non-coding RNAs have also been shown to fine-tune the activation and function of developmental regulators, including transcription factors responsible for maintenance of pluripotency (Sheik Mohamed et al., 2010; Ulitsky et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2012), mesoderm specification (Frank et al., 2019) and neuronal differentiation (Xi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Frank et al., 2019)

claim: Long non-coding RNAs have been shown to fine-tune the activation and function of developmental regulators involved in neuronal differentiation.
source: More specifically, long non-coding RNAs have also been shown to fine-tune the activation and function of developmental regulators, including transcription factors responsible for maintenance of pluripotency (Sheik Mohamed et al., 2010; Ulitsky et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2012), mesoderm specification (Frank et al., 2019) and neuronal differentiation (Xi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Xi et al., 2022)

claim: Recent studies have attributed critical roles for lncRNAs in the early stages of human development, in particular during definitive endoderm specification through cis-regulatory activity on nearby genes.
source: Recent studies have also attributed critical roles for lncRNAs in the early stages of human development, in particular during definitive endoderm specification through cis-regulatory activity on nearby genes (Jiang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Jiang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2020)

claim: LNC00261 facilitates the activation of the proximal FOXA2 gene via association with SMAD2/3.
source: For instance, LNC00261 facilitates the activation of the proximal FOXA2 gene via association with SMAD2/3 (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Jiang et al., 2015)

claim: A mechanistically similar cis-regulation of GATA6 has been attributed to lncRNA GATA6-AS1.
source: A mechanistically similar cis-regulation of GATA6 has been attributed to lncRNA GATA6-AS1 (Yang et al., 2020), while the lncRNA DIGIT has been reported to control GSC in trans-, via the formation of BRD3-dependent phase-separated condensates (Daneshvar et al., 2016; Daneshvar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Yang et al., 2020)

claim: The lncRNA DIGIT has been reported to control GSC in trans-, via the formation of BRD3-dependent phase-separated condensates.
source: A mechanistically similar cis-regulation of GATA6 has been attributed to lncRNA GATA6-AS1 (Yang et al., 2020), while the lncRNA DIGIT has been reported to control GSC in trans-, via the formation of BRD3-dependent phase-separated condensates (Daneshvar et al., 2016; Daneshvar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Daneshvar et al., 2016; Daneshvar et al., 2020)

claim: The majority of lncRNAs exhibit highly tissue-specific expression, often more restricted than observed for protein-coding genes.
source: The majority of lncRNAs exhibit highly tissue-specific expression, often more restricted than observed for protein-coding genes (Cabili et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Cabili et al., 2011)

claim: Signaling molecules, including TGF-β, WNT and the JUN/JNK/AP-pathway represent critical cascades necessary for endoderm formation.
source: Signaling molecules, including TGF-β, WNT and the JUN/JNK/AP-pathway represent critical cascades necessary for endoderm formation, inducing the expression of endodermal factors such as SOX17, GATA6 and C-X-C chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4) (Li et al., 2019; Chia et al., 2019; Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Li et al., 2019; Chia et al., 2019; Fisher et al., 2017)

claim: Signaling molecules necessary for endoderm formation induce the expression of endodermal factors such as SOX17, GATA6 and C-X-C chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4).
source: Signaling molecules, including TGF-β, WNT and the JUN/JNK/AP-pathway represent critical cascades necessary for endoderm formation, inducing the expression of endodermal factors such as SOX17, GATA6 and C-X-C chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4) (Li et al., 2019; Chia et al., 2019; Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Li et al., 2019; Chia et al., 2019; Fisher et al., 2017)

claim: SOX17 is a member of the SOX-F group of transcription factors.
source: SOX17 is a member of the SOX-F group of transcription factors and its expression is necessary for the specification of definitive endoderm in vitro (Séguin et al., 2008) and in vivo (Kanai-Azuma et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about SOX17 classification

claim: SOX17 expression is necessary for the specification of definitive endoderm in vitro.
source: SOX17 is a member of the SOX-F group of transcription factors and its expression is necessary for the specification of definitive endoderm in vitro (Séguin et al., 2008) and in vivo (Kanai-Azuma et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Séguin et al., 2008)

claim: SOX17 expression is necessary for the specification of definitive endoderm in vivo.
source: SOX17 is a member of the SOX-F group of transcription factors and its expression is necessary for the specification of definitive endoderm in vitro (Séguin et al., 2008) and in vivo (Kanai-Azuma et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Kanai-Azuma et al., 2002)

claim: SOX17 is the only annotated gene located within the 336 kb SOX17 loop-domain insulated by strong CTCF-boundaries.
source: So far, SOX17 is the only annotated gene located within the 336 kb SOX17 loop-domain insulated by strong CTCF-boundaries (Figure 1A, top).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and analysis of the genomic region

claim: The combination of histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) and histone H3 lysine 36 trimethylation (H3K36me3) in ESC-derived endoderm suggested the presence of an RNA Polymerase-II-driven transcript.
source: In particular, the combination of histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) and histone H3 lysine 36 trimethylation (H3K36me3) in ESC-derived endoderm suggested the presence of an RNA Polymerase-II-driven transcript (Guttman et al., 2009; Bilodeau et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Guttman et al., 2009; Bilodeau et al., 2009) and inference from histone modification patterns

claim: Matched RNA sequencing data showed a 22 kb long transcribed region approximately 230 kb upstream of SOX17.
source: Further supporting this, matched RNA sequencing data showed a 22 kb long transcribed region approximately 230 kb upstream of SOX17 (Figure 1A, bottom).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The transcribed region approximately 230 kb upstream of SOX17 combined with a strong UCSC PhyloCSF sequence conservation points to an intergenic lncRNA termed T-REX17.
source: These results combined with a strong UCSC PhyloCSF sequence conservation points to an intergenic lncRNA (lincRNA) that we subsequently termed T-REX17 (Transcript Regulating Endoderm and activated by soX17) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data, sequence conservation analysis, and histone modification patterns shown in Figures 1A and 1B

claim: The sequence conservation of T-REX17 to the mouse is only modest.
source: Although the sequence conservation to the mouse is only modest (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we detect the presence of a distal SOX17 transcript in a number of vertebrates based on stage- and tissue-matched embryonic data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: A distal SOX17 transcript is present in a number of vertebrates based on stage- and tissue-matched embryonic data.
source: Although the sequence conservation to the mouse is only modest (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we detect the presence of a distal SOX17 transcript in a number of vertebrates based on stage- and tissue-matched embryonic data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from multiple vertebrate species shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Two distinct sites with notable transcription factor (TF) occupancy were found within a region of open chromatin specifically in definitive endoderm at the distal regulatory element.
source: We found two distinct sites with notable transcription factor (TF) occupancy within a region of open chromatin specifically in definitive endoderm (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Both sites at the distal regulatory element show enriched UCSC PhyloCSF sequence conservation and are characterized by a distinguishable promoter and enhancer signature.
source: Although both sites show enriched UCSC PhyloCSF sequence conservation, they are also characterized by a distinguishable promoter and enhancer signature (ChromHMM state 22 and ChromHMM state 13, respectively) (Figure 1B; Ernst and Kellis, 2012; Ernst and Kellis, 2017).
evidence: Supported by sequence conservation data and ChromHMM analysis shown in Figure 1B, with citations to Ernst and Kellis, 2012; Ernst and Kellis, 2017

claim: The putative promoter region of T-REX17 (pT-REX17) is endoderm-specific in a luciferase assay.
source: We next assessed the activity of the putative promoter region of T-REX17 (pT-REX17) in a luciferase assay and found it to be endoderm-specific (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: The entire putative enhancer region and eSOX17.2 alone showed strong enhancer activity during endoderm differentiation.
source: The entire region but also eSOX17.2 alone showed strong enhancer activity during endoderm differentiation (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Cas9-induced homozygous deletions of eSOX17.2 resulted in a delayed activation of SOX17 and overall reduced expression of CXCR4.
source: We then further evaluated eSOX17.2 function using Cas9-induced homozygous deletions and assessed the effect of the mutation during directed endoderm differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E). Interestingly, we observed a delayed activation of SOX17 and overall reduced expression of the transmembrane C-X-C chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G following Cas9-mediated deletion

claim: 4C-seq on pluripotent cells and early endoderm found an enriched interaction between the SOX17 promoter and its distal enhancer (eSOX17).
source: To investigate the physical interactions at the locus, we performed Circularized Chromosome Conformation Capture sequencing (4C-seq) on pluripotent cells and early endoderm and found an enriched interaction between the SOX17 promoter and its distal enhancer (eSOX17) (Figure 1D and E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 1D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H

claim: The topologically isolated domain of SOX17 encompasses a distal, transcribed region driven by a promoter in close proximity but otherwise independent from a functional enhancer that interacts with the SOX17 gene.
source: Therefore, we can conclude that the topologically isolated domain of SOX17 encompasses a distal, transcribed region driven by a promoter in close proximity but otherwise independent from a functional enhancer that interacts with the SOX17 gene.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of 4C-seq, luciferase assays, and deletion experiments

claim: T-REX17 expression follows SOX17 kinetics but with an approximate 24 hour delay.
source: We next investigated the expression of the non-coding transcript during endoderm differentiation with time-resolved qRT-PCR and found that T-REX17 expression follows SOX17 kinetics but with an approximate 24 hour delay (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by time-resolved qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A

claim: T-REX17 appears tightly restricted to early human definitive endoderm and uncoupled from the much broader expression of SOX17 in many other endoderm-derived tissues.
source: T-REX17 appears tightly restricted to early human definitive endoderm and, importantly, uncoupled from the much broader expression of SOX17 in many other endoderm-derived tissues (Mathias et al., 2015, Thul et al., 2017; Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data across multiple tissues shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C, with citations to Mathias et al., 2015, Thul et al., 2017

claim: T-REX17 is not expressed during mesoderm and ectoderm formation.
source: Moreover, we utilized RNA-seq data from the three pluripotent stem cell-derived germ layers to show that T-REX17 is not expressed during mesoderm and ectoderm formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: scRNAseq data in the early human gastrulating embryo confirms T-REX17's tissue specificity in vivo.
source: scRNAseq data in the early human gastrulating embryo (Tyser et al., 2021) confirms T-REX17's tissue specificity in vivo (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, with citation to Tyser et al., 2021

claim: T-REX17 is highly enriched at foci within the nuclear compartment as shown by single-molecule RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (smRNA-FISH).
source: We also investigated T-REX17 localization by single-molecule RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (smRNA-FISH) and found it highly enriched at foci within the nuclear compartment, a characteristic feature of non-coding transcripts (median of 40 foci/cell, Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: Nuclear localization and association with chromatin of T-REX17 were confirmed by cell-fractionation experiments.
source: Nuclear localization and association with chromatin were further confirmed by cell-fractionation experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by cell fractionation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: 37 of 40 predicted open reading frames (ORFs) in T-REX17 would likely result in no functional protein according to PhyloCSF analysis.
source: Next, we wanted to more closely inspect the coding potential of T-REX17 and used PhyloCSF to show that 37 of 40 predicted open reading frames (ORFs) would likely result in no functional protein (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by PhyloCSF analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: The coding potential of T-REX17 ORFs is comparable to other short ORFs (sORFs) in the human lncRNA catalog.
source: This is comparable to other short ORFs (sORFs) in the human lncRNA catalog (Figure 2E; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by comparison to lncRNA catalog data shown in Figure 2E, with citation to Lin et al., 2011

claim: The coding potential of the three remaining T-REX17 sORFs is about two orders of magnitude lower than for the SOX17 coding sequence.
source: Notably, even the coding potential of the remaining three sORFs is about two orders of magnitude lower than for the SOX17 coding sequence (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by PhyloCSF analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: The two most prevalent T-REX17 isoforms account for 23.3% of the split-reads from long-read Nanopore sequencing.
source: The two most prevalent isoforms account for 23.3% of the split-reads, while 76.7% appear inconsistently spliced, a feature which is frequently observed in lncRNAs (Mukherjee et al., 2017; Lagarde et al., 2017; Schlackow et al., 2017; Struhl, 2007; Beck et al., 2016) (termed 'sloppy' splicing, Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by Nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: 76.7% of T-REX17 transcripts appear inconsistently spliced, a feature which is frequently observed in lncRNAs.
source: The two most prevalent isoforms account for 23.3% of the split-reads, while 76.7% appear inconsistently spliced, a feature which is frequently observed in lncRNAs (Mukherjee et al., 2017; Lagarde et al., 2017; Schlackow et al., 2017; Struhl, 2007; Beck et al., 2016) (termed 'sloppy' splicing, Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by Nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, with citations to published literature (Mukherjee et al., 2017; Lagarde et al., 2017; Schlackow et al., 2017; Struhl, 2007; Beck et al., 2016)

claim: 5' and 3' RACE were used to determine the exact transcriptional start and end sites as well as the corresponding polyadenylation signal of T-REX17.
source: Additionally, we used 5' and 3' rapid amplification of cDNA end (RACE) to determine the exact transcriptional start and end sites as well as the corresponding polyadenylation signal (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by RACE data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H

claim: T-REX17 is specifically and transiently expressed in early definitive endoderm.
source: Taken together, our results show that T-REX17 is specifically and transiently expressed in early definitive endoderm and creates a 'sloppy spliced' nuclear transcript.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of expression analysis, localization studies, and sequencing data

claim: T-REX17 creates a 'sloppy spliced' nuclear transcript.
source: Taken together, our results show that T-REX17 is specifically and transiently expressed in early definitive endoderm and creates a 'sloppy spliced' nuclear transcript.
evidence: Supported by Nanopore sequencing and smRNA-FISH data

claim: dCas9-mediated silencing resulted in a strong repression of T-REX17 RNA compared to the control.
source: The dCas9-mediated silencing resulted in a strong repression of T-REX17 RNA compared to the control, which we further validated by smRNA-FISH (Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3B, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: H3K9me3 enrichment was detected around the T-REX17 promoter in sgT-REX17 cells, with a certain degree of spreading toward the enhancer eSOX17 but no apparent consequence on SOX17 regulation.
source: We furthermore detected H3K9me3 enrichment around the T-REX17 promoter in sgT-REX17 cells, with a certain degree of spreading toward the enhancer eSOX17 but no apparent consequence on SOX17 regulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by H3K9me3 ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Capture Hi-C in both cell lines could not observe any significant interaction differences within the SOX17-loop domain in definitive endoderm.
source: To assess possible effects of the T-REX17 depletion on SOX17, we performed Capture Hi-C (cHi-C) in both cell lines, but could not observe any significant interaction differences (Log2FC = 0.02 p=0.049) within the SOX17-loop domain in definitive endoderm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Capture Hi-C data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: Virtual 4C analysis revealed a marginal decrease in the SOX17 enhancer-promoter interaction in the absence of T-REX17.
source: Nevertheless, virtual 4C analysis revealed a marginal decrease in the SOX17 enhancer-promoter interaction in the absence of T-REX17 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by virtual 4C analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: Loss of T-REX17 does not appear to affect SOX17 transcriptional activation and expression levels, indicating preserved enhancer functionality.
source: Despite this limited topological difference, loss of T-REX17 does not appear to affect SOX17 transcriptional activation and expression levels, indicating preserved enhancer functionality (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D and E

claim: Unrelated genes present in neighboring domains were unaffected by the T-REX17 perturbation.
source: We also confirmed that unrelated genes present in neighboring domains were unaffected by the perturbation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: SOX17 occupancy at the SOX17 locus and genome-wide is largely unaffected by the loss of T-REX17.
source: Next, we performed SOX17 Chromatin Immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) and show that SOX17 occupancy at the SOX17 locus (including at its induced heterochromatic distal enhancer (eSOX17)) as well as genome-wide is largely unaffected by the loss of T-REX17 (Figure 3D and F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by SOX17 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3D, F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: SOX17 enrichment was found at the T-REX17 promoter (pT-REX17), potentially contributing to its activation.
source: Interestingly, we found SOX17 enrichment at the T-REX17 promoter (pT-REX17), potentially contributing to its activation and consistent with the timing relative to SOX17 (Figures 3D, G ,, 2A).
evidence: Supported by SOX17 ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 3D and G, and inferred from timing data in Figure 2A

claim: Homozygous SOX17 knock-out cells fail to induce the expression of the endoderm master regulator GATA4.
source: Notably, homozygous knock-out cells fail to induce the expression of the endoderm master regulator GATA4, and show no activation of T-REX17 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J

claim: Homozygous SOX17 knock-out cells show no activation of T-REX17.
source: Notably, homozygous knock-out cells fail to induce the expression of the endoderm master regulator GATA4, and show no activation of T-REX17 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J

claim: The expression of T-REX17 is abolished in T-REX17p(A)/p(A) EN cells, while the mRuby cassette is actively transcribed, indicating ongoing transcription at the locus in an endoderm-specific manner.
source: qRT-PCR demonstrated that the expression of T-REX17 is abolished in T-REX17p(A)/p(A) EN cells, while the mRuby cassette is actively transcribed, indicating ongoing transcription at the locus in an endoderm-specific manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1N

claim: SOX17 expression levels are not affected in T-REX17p(A)/p(A) EN cells.
source: In line with our depletion experiments, SOX17 expression levels are not affected in T-REX17p(A)/p(A) EN cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1N

claim: T-REX17 induction is dependent on SOX17.
source: These results demonstrate that T-REX17 induction is dependent on SOX17, whereas the T-REX17 transcript and the act of transcription are dispensable for SOX17 activation as well as its genome-wide localization.
evidence: Inferred from SOX17 knock-out and ChIP-seq experiments

claim: The T-REX17 transcript and the act of transcription are dispensable for SOX17 activation as well as its genome-wide localization.
source: These results demonstrate that T-REX17 induction is dependent on SOX17, whereas the T-REX17 transcript and the act of transcription are dispensable for SOX17 activation as well as its genome-wide localization.
evidence: Inferred from T-REX17 depletion and early termination experiments showing no effect on SOX17

claim: RNA-pulldown followed by mass spectrometry identified several heterogenous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP) family members, including HNRNPU, as putative T-REX17 interactors.
source: To this end, we performed RNA-pulldown followed by mass spectrometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B). Among the putative T-REX17 interactors, we identified several heterogenous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP) family members, including HNRNPU (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: HNRNPU was previously reported to interact with lncRNAs to regulate various functions during development including nuclear matrix organization.
source: HNRNPU waspreviously reported to interact with lncRNAs to regulate various functions during development including nuclear matrix organization (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Alvarez-Dominguez et al., 2017), X chromosome inactivation (Hasegawa et al., 2010), RNA splicing (Xiao et al., 2012; Huelga et al., 2012), and epigenetic control of gene expression (Khyzha et al., 2019; Song et al., 2020; Puvvula et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Alvarez-Dominguez et al., 2017)

claim: HNRNPU was previously reported to interact with lncRNAs to regulate X chromosome inactivation.
source: HNRNPU waspreviously reported to interact with lncRNAs to regulate various functions during development including nuclear matrix organization (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Alvarez-Dominguez et al., 2017), X chromosome inactivation (Hasegawa et al., 2010), RNA splicing (Xiao et al., 2012; Huelga et al., 2012), and epigenetic control of gene expression (Khyzha et al., 2019; Song et al., 2020; Puvvula et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Hasegawa et al., 2010)

claim: HNRNPU was previously reported to interact with lncRNAs to regulate RNA splicing.
source: HNRNPU waspreviously reported to interact with lncRNAs to regulate various functions during development including nuclear matrix organization (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Alvarez-Dominguez et al., 2017), X chromosome inactivation (Hasegawa et al., 2010), RNA splicing (Xiao et al., 2012; Huelga et al., 2012), and epigenetic control of gene expression (Khyzha et al., 2019; Song et al., 2020; Puvvula et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Xiao et al., 2012; Huelga et al., 2012)

claim: HNRNPU was previously reported to interact with lncRNAs to regulate epigenetic control of gene expression.
source: HNRNPU waspreviously reported to interact with lncRNAs to regulate various functions during development including nuclear matrix organization (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Alvarez-Dominguez et al., 2017), X chromosome inactivation (Hasegawa et al., 2010), RNA splicing (Xiao et al., 2012; Huelga et al., 2012), and epigenetic control of gene expression (Khyzha et al., 2019; Song et al., 2020; Puvvula et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Khyzha et al., 2019; Song et al., 2020; Puvvula et al., 2014)

claim: HNRNPU RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) found T-REX17 to be enriched to levels comparable to known RNA interactors such as XIST or NEAT1.
source: To validate HNRNPU-T-REX17 interaction, we performed HNRNPU RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E) and found T-REX17 to be enriched to levels comparable to known RNA interactors such as XIST or NEAT1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by RIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, E, and F

claim: T-REX17-depleted cells showed a substantial reduction in the CXCR4+ cell population during differentiation.
source: To investigate the cellular role of T-REX17, we performed immunofluorescent staining and fluorescent activated cell sorting (FACS) for CXCR4 in control and T-REX17-depleted cells. The latter showed a substantial reduction in the CXCR4+ cell population during differentiation, suggesting hampered differentiation potential toward endoderm (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4A

claim: SOX17 protein levels were not affected in T-REX17-depleted cells.
source: However, consistent with the transcriptional data, SOX17 protein levels were not affected (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The CXCR4 reduction phenotype was recapitulated in the T-REX17p(A)/p(A) EN cells.
source: Both phenotypes were recapitulated in the T-REX17p(A)/p(A) EN cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Differentiation toward mesoderm and ectoderm was not affected by T-REX17 loss.
source: As expected, based on its highly restricted expression, differentiation toward the other two germ layers (mesoderm and ectoderm) was not affected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D

claim: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) revealed only marginal variance by day 3 of endoderm differentiation between T-REX17 depleted and control cell lines.
source: Next, we performed time-resolved RNA-seq in T-REX17 depleted and control cell lines on days 0, 3, and 5 of endoderm differentiation. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) revealed only marginal variance by day 3, while a more substantial transcriptional divergence was observed on day 5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: A more substantial transcriptional divergence was observed on day 5 of endoderm differentiation between T-REX17 depleted and control cell lines.
source: Next, we performed time-resolved RNA-seq in T-REX17 depleted and control cell lines on days 0, 3, and 5 of endoderm differentiation. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) revealed only marginal variance by day 3, while a more substantial transcriptional divergence was observed on day 5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: Differential gene expression analysis identified 584 significantly down- and 590 significantly upregulated genes in T-REX17-depleted cells at day 5.
source: Differential gene expression analysis identified 584 significantly down- and 590 significantly upregulated genes in T-REX17-depleted cells at day 5 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Pluripotency genes (e.g. POU5F1, NANOG) were found to be significantly upregulated in T-REX17-depleted cells.
source: In particular, we found pluripotency genes (e.g. POU5F1, NANOG) and endoderm/WNT-related genes (e.g. EOMES, GATA3, CXCR4, FZD5, FZD7, FZD8, DKK1, NOTUM, ROR1, CXXC4, SFRP5) to be significantly up- and downregulated, respectively (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Endoderm/WNT-related genes (e.g. EOMES, GATA3, CXCR4, FZD5, FZD7, FZD8, DKK1, NOTUM, ROR1, CXXC4, SFRP5) were found to be significantly downregulated in T-REX17-depleted cells.
source: In particular, we found pluripotency genes (e.g. POU5F1, NANOG) and endoderm/WNT-related genes (e.g. EOMES, GATA3, CXCR4, FZD5, FZD7, FZD8, DKK1, NOTUM, ROR1, CXXC4, SFRP5) to be significantly up- and downregulated, respectively (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Time resolved qPCR analysis confirmed a lack of key endoderm markers activation and expression in T-REX17-depleted cells (including CXCR4, GATA3, GATA4, KLF5, CPE, GPR, HHEX, EPSTI1, FOXA3).
source: Time resolved qPCR analysis over 5 days confirmed, a lack of key endoderm markers activation and expression in T-REX17-depleted cells (including CXCR4, GATA3, GATA4, KLF5, CPE, GPR, HHEX, EPSTI1, FOXA3), an aberrant transcriptional signature we also observe in T-REX17p(A)/p(A) EN cells (Martinez Barbera et al., 2000; Grapin-Botton and Constam, 2007; McLean et al., 2007; Séguin et al., 2008; Teo et al., 2011; Aksoy et al., 2014; Dettmer et al., 2020; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H, with citations to published literature (Martinez Barbera et al., 2000; Grapin-Botton and Constam, 2007; McLean et al., 2007; Séguin et al., 2008; Teo et al., 2011; Aksoy et al., 2014; Dettmer et al., 2020)

claim: An aberrant transcriptional signature was observed in T-REX17p(A)/p(A) EN cells.
source: Time resolved qPCR analysis over 5 days confirmed, a lack of key endoderm markers activation and expression in T-REX17-depleted cells (including CXCR4, GATA3, GATA4, KLF5, CPE, GPR, HHEX, EPSTI1, FOXA3), an aberrant transcriptional signature we also observe in T-REX17p(A)/p(A) EN cells (Martinez Barbera et al., 2000; Grapin-Botton and Constam, 2007; McLean et al., 2007; Séguin et al., 2008; Teo et al., 2011; Aksoy et al., 2014; Dettmer et al., 2020; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H

claim: Among the significantly upregulated genes in T-REX17-depleted cells, there was an enrichment of JUN (AP-1) pathway target genes (including EGR1, ATF3, PVR, DAB2, NOTCH2, MFHAS1, SPARC).
source: Interestingly, among the significantly, upregulated genes in T-REX17-depleted cells, we found an enrichment of JUN (AP-1) pathway target genes (including EGR1, ATF3, PVR, DAB2, NOTCH2, MFHAS1, SPARC) (Briggs et al., 2002; Schummer et al., 2016; Florin et al., 2004; van Dam and Castellazzi, 2001; Hoffmann et al., 2008; Kockel et al., 2001), which has recently been described to act as a barrier for the exit from pluripotency toward endoderm formation (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, with citations to published literature (Briggs et al., 2002; Schummer et al., 2016; Florin et al., 2004; van Dam and Castellazzi, 2001; Hoffmann et al., 2008; Kockel et al., 2001; Li et al., 2019)

claim: The JUN pathway has recently been described to act as a barrier for the exit from pluripotency toward endoderm formation.
source: Interestingly, among the significantly, upregulated genes in T-REX17-depleted cells, we found an enrichment of JUN (AP-1) pathway target genes (including EGR1, ATF3, PVR, DAB2, NOTCH2, MFHAS1, SPARC) (Briggs et al., 2002; Schummer et al., 2016; Florin et al., 2004; van Dam and Castellazzi, 2001; Hoffmann et al., 2008; Kockel et al., 2001), which has recently been described to act as a barrier for the exit from pluripotency toward endoderm formation (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Li et al., 2019)

claim: Increased relative amounts of pJNK were observed in T-REX17-depleted cells.
source: Phosphorylation levels of JUN-activating upstream kinase JNK are a strong indicator of JUN pathway activation (Raivich and Behrens, 2006; Muniyappa and Das, 2008; Li et al., 2019), which we observed by increased relative amounts of pJNK in T-REX17-depleted cells (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, with citations to published literature (Raivich and Behrens, 2006; Muniyappa and Das, 2008; Li et al., 2019)

claim: Inhibition of JNK hyperactivity from day 3 of definitive endoderm differentiation partially rescued the specification defect in T-REX17-depleted cells.
source: Inhibition of JNK hyperactivity (JNK Inhibitor XVI) from day 3 of definitive endoderm differentiation partially rescued the specification defect in T-REX17-depleted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and FACS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C

claim: Immunofluorescent staining for ECAD, NCAD, and VIM revealed retention of an epithelial signature in T-REX17 depleted endoderm cells.
source: Furthermore, immunofluorescent staining for ECAD, NCAD, and VIM revealed retention of an epithelial signature in T-REX17 depleted endoderm cells (Figure 4D and E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D, E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E

claim: VIM-signal distribution within T-REX17-depleted cells was altered, indicating a potential cellular polarization defect.
source: Moreover, VIM-signal distribution within T-REX17-depleted cells was also altered, indicating a potential cellular polarization defect (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E

claim: A very distinct PDX1+ population was identified in the control cell population after 9 days of directed differentiation, which is notably reduced in T-REX17-depleted cells.
source: Finally, we evaluated if T-REX17-depleted cells have lost the potential to further differentiate into pancreatic progenitor (PP) cells (Alvarez-Dominguez et al., 2020). Immunofluorescent staining identified a very distinct PDX1+ population in the control cell population after 9 days of directed differentiation, which is notably reduced in T-REX17-depleted cells (Figure 4F and G; Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F, G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F, with citation to Alvarez-Dominguez et al., 2020

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of differentiated control and T-REX17-depleted cells indicates a substantial gene expression difference, including the specific downregulation of pancreatic progenitor marker genes.
source: In addition, transcriptomic analysis of differentiated control and T-REX17-depleted cells indicates a substantial gene expression difference, including the specific downregulation of pancreatic progenitor marker genes (Alvarez-Dominguez et al., 2020; Figure 4H; Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2G, with citation to Alvarez-Dominguez et al., 2020

claim: T-REX17 is important for the induction of definitive endoderm, which directly impacts the subsequent differentiation potential.
source: Our data therefore highlight the importance of T-REX17 for the induction of definitive endoderm, which directly impacts the subsequent differentiation potential.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing reduced endoderm markers, impaired pancreatic differentiation, and altered signaling in T-REX17-depleted cells

claim: Most lncRNAs act locally, regulating the chromatin architecture and the expression of neighboring genes in cis-.
source: Here, we describe the discovery and characterization of T-REX17 as a functionally essential lncRNA in human definitive endoderm. Most lncRNAs act locally, regulating the chromatin architecture and the expression of neighboring genes in cis- (Tan et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011; Goff et al., 2015; Engreitz et al., 2016), especially when overlapping with enhancer elements.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Tan et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011; Goff et al., 2015; Engreitz et al., 2016)

claim: The fine-tuned expression of several developmental transcription factors has been shown to rely on the activity of lncRNAs present within the same topological domain.
source: In particular, the fine-tuned expression of several developmental transcription factors has been shown to rely on the activity of lncRNAs present within the same topological domain (Wang et al., 2011; Frank et al., 2019; Messemaker et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Wang et al., 2011; Frank et al., 2019; Messemaker et al., 2018)

claim: T-REX17 appears distinct from other endodermal specific lncRNAs as it does not appear to regulate the adjacent SOX17 gene.
source: Interestingly, T-REX17 appears distinct from these and other endodermal specific lncRNAs (Jiang et al., 2015; Liao et al., 2019; Daneshvar et al., 2016) as it does not appear to regulate the adjacent SOX17 gene.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing no effect on SOX17 expression upon T-REX17 loss, with citations to other endodermal lncRNAs (Jiang et al., 2015; Liao et al., 2019; Daneshvar et al., 2016)

claim: The use of two orthogonal loss of function approaches showed that T-REX17 transcription is dispensable for proper SOX17 regulation.
source: The use of two orthogonal loss of function approaches in our work (suppression of T-REX17 activation and early termination) showed that T-REX17 transcription is dispensable for proper SOX17 regulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from both dCas9-KRAB-MeCP2 silencing and early termination experiments

claim: T-REX17 may regulate distant and unrelated loci to the SOX17 loop-domain, as many T-REX17 distinct puncta are found in the nuclear compartment of endodermal cells.
source: It remains to be determined what the targets and regulatory mechanism of T-REX17 are. One may speculate that these could be distant and unrelated loci to the SOX17 loop-domain, as we find many T-REX17 distinct puncta in the nuclear compartment of endodermal cells.
evidence: Speculative inference based on smRNA-FISH observations showing multiple nuclear foci

claim: Local cis-acting lncRNAs mainly show accumulation at the two sites of nascent transcription.
source: Typically, local cis-acting lncRNAs mainly show accumulation at the two sites of nascent transcription (Jiang et al., 2015; Lewandowski et al., 2019; Daneshvar et al., 2016; Daneshvar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Jiang et al., 2015; Lewandowski et al., 2019; Daneshvar et al., 2016; Daneshvar et al., 2020)

claim: The observed interaction with the HNRNP complex may link T-REX17 to various nuclear-related functions needed for endoderm specification.
source: The observed interaction with the HNRNP complex may link it to various nuclear-related functions needed for endoderm specification.
evidence: Speculative inference based on HNRNPU interaction data

claim: Other endodermal lncRNAs mainly exert their functions together with endoderm-specific transcription factors.
source: It will be interesting to see how this compares to other endodermal lncRNAs, which mainly exert their functions together with endoderm-specific transcription factors (Jiang et al., 2015; Daneshvar et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Jiang et al., 2015; Daneshvar et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020)

claim: SOX genes are fundamental transcription factors that have a variety of functions including the specification of cell types and tissues during embryonic development.
source: SOX genes are fundamental transcription factors that have a variety of functions including the specification of cell types and tissues during embryonic development.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about SOX genes

claim: SOX genes are evolutionary conserved and evolved as a result of a series of ancient genomic duplication events.
source: They are evolutionary conserved and evolved as a result of a series of ancient genomic duplication events (Bowles et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bowles et al., 2000)

claim: At other SOX gene loci, the presence of one or multiple lncRNAs have been reported, but these lncRNAs appear involved in the modulation of the associated SOX gene expression in cis-.
source: Interestingly, at other SOX gene loci, the presence of one or multiple lncRNAs have been reported, but these lncRNAs, in contrast to T-REX17, appear involved in the modulation of the associated SOX gene expression in cis- (Tariq et al., 2020; Barter et al., 2017; Amaral et al., 2009; Ahmad et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Tariq et al., 2020; Barter et al., 2017; Amaral et al., 2009; Ahmad et al., 2017)

claim: lncRNAs near paralogous genes may evolve distinct role and regulatory mechanisms.
source: This suggests that lncRNAs near paralogous genes may evolve distinct role and regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of T-REX17 function with other SOX-associated lncRNAs

claim: T-REX17 is essential for definitive endoderm specification.
source: At a functional level, our results show that T-REX17 is essential for definitive endoderm specification and its loss limits further downstream differentiation, as demonstrated by the pancreatic progenitor differentiation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing impaired endoderm markers and differentiation upon T-REX17 loss

claim: T-REX17 loss limits further downstream differentiation, as demonstrated by the pancreatic progenitor differentiation.
source: At a functional level, our results show that T-REX17 is essential for definitive endoderm specification and its loss limits further downstream differentiation, as demonstrated by the pancreatic progenitor differentiation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced PDX1+ cells and pancreatic marker expression

claim: T-REX17 has a transient, highly stage-specific nature compared to most protein-coding genes, including endodermal transcription factors.
source: From the developmental perspective, T-REX17 and its transient, highly stage-specific nature make it an intriguing regulator compared to most of the protein-coding genes, including endodermal transcription factors, for example SOX17, FOXA2, and GATA4, which are expressed longer and in a variety of somatic tissues.
evidence: Supported by expression data showing T-REX17 is restricted to early endoderm while SOX17, FOXA2, and GATA4 are expressed more broadly

claim: The development of definitive endoderm during human gastrulation in vivo takes place within hours.
source: In this context, it is worth noting that the development of definitive endoderm during human gastrulation in vivo takes place within hours and the gene regulatory network (GRN) governing this transition has to be tightly controlled (Tsankov et al., 2015; Gifford et al., 2013; Chia et al., 2019), which could also involve lncRNAs such as T-REX17.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Tsankov et al., 2015; Gifford et al., 2013; Chia et al., 2019)

claim: The gene regulatory network (GRN) governing definitive endoderm transition has to be tightly controlled.
source: In this context, it is worth noting that the development of definitive endoderm during human gastrulation in vivo takes place within hours and the gene regulatory network (GRN) governing this transition has to be tightly controlled (Tsankov et al., 2015; Gifford et al., 2013; Chia et al., 2019), which could also involve lncRNAs such as T-REX17.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Tsankov et al., 2015; Gifford et al., 2013; Chia et al., 2019)

claim: The gene regulatory network governing definitive endoderm transition could involve lncRNAs such as T-REX17.
source: In this context, it is worth noting that the development of definitive endoderm during human gastrulation in vivo takes place within hours and the gene regulatory network (GRN) governing this transition has to be tightly controlled (Tsankov et al., 2015; Gifford et al., 2013; Chia et al., 2019), which could also involve lncRNAs such as T-REX17.
evidence: Speculative inference based on T-REX17's essential role in endoderm formation
